title: Given an array of integers that may include negatives and a target k, find the length of the shortest contiguous non-empty subarray whose sum is at least k, returning minus one if none exists. Solve it with prefix sums and a monotonic deque and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Challenge: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K (Prefix Sums with a Monotonic Deque)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks for the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least k, in an array that may contain negatives. Because negatives break the simple sliding window, it is solved in linear time with prefix sums and a monotonically increasing deque of prefix-sum indices: for each new prefix we pop from the front while the window qualifies to record candidate lengths, and pop from the back any prefix that is not smaller than the current one, since such prefixes can never be a better left endpoint.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a sequence of daily net cash flows that can be positive or negative and wants the fewest consecutive days whose total reaches at least a target. Because a negative day can sink a running total, the simple trimming trick fails. Instead he keeps a tidy ordered list of candidate starting points, discards any starting point that is worse than a newer one, and from the front he confirms and removes starting points as soon as the stretch to today reaches the target.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use prefix sums with a deque that stays increasing, popping the front when the window qualifies and the back when a newer prefix is not larger.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem asks for the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least k, in an array that may contain negatives. Because negatives break the simple sliding window, it is solved in linear time with prefix sums and a monotonically increasing deque of prefix-sum indices: for each new prefix we pop from the front while the window qualifies to record candidate lengths, and pop from the back any prefix that is not smaller than the current one, since such prefixes can never be a better left endpoint.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a sequence of daily net cash flows that can be positive or negative and wants the fewest consecutive days whose total reaches at least a target. Because a negative day can sink a running total, the simple trimming trick fails. Instead he keeps a tidy ordered list of candidate starting points, discards any starting point that is worse than a newer one, and from the front he confirms and removes starting points as soon as the stretch to today reaches the target.

**One line to remember:** Use prefix sums with a deque that stays increasing, popping the front when the window qualifies and the back when a newer prefix is not larger.

sections.s2_technical:
With possibly negative numbers the greedy positive-only window does not work, because shrinking from the left can both increase and decrease the sum unpredictably. The robust approach uses prefix sums. Let P be the array of prefix sums where P at index i is the sum of the first i elements, with P at zero being zero. The sum of the subarray from index j to index i minus one is P at i minus P at j, and we want the shortest such span with P at i minus P at j at least k.

For each right endpoint i we want the largest j less than i with P at j no more than P at i minus k, because that gives the shortest qualifying subarray ending at i. We process the prefix sums left to right maintaining a double-ended queue of indices whose prefix values are strictly increasing from front to back. Two operations keep it correct. First, from the front, while the deque is non-empty and P at i minus P at the front index is at least k, we have a qualifying subarray, so we record the length i minus the front index and pop the front, because any later right endpoint would only give a longer subarray with this same left endpoint. Second, from the back, while the deque is non-empty and P at the back index is greater than or equal to P at i, we pop the back, because the current prefix is smaller or equal and at a later index, making it a strictly better left-endpoint candidate for everyone to come.

After those two steps we push the current index onto the back of the deque. The front pops give candidate lengths from which we keep the minimum. The reason this is linear is that each index is pushed once and popped at most once across the entire run, so the total deque work is bounded by 2n. The senior-level nuance is understanding why both pops are valid: front pops because a qualified left endpoint is never needed again, and back pops because a higher earlier prefix is dominated by a lower later one.

We use long prefix sums to avoid overflow, and we return minus one if no front pop ever produced a qualifying length. The time complexity is linear, O(n), and the space complexity is O(n) for the prefix sums and the deque. This prefix-sum-with-monotonic-deque method is the canonical solution for shortest-subarray-with-sum-at-least-k on signed arrays and is a notable step up in difficulty from the positive-only window.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the intraday-liquidity desk reviews a sequence of net cash movements that can be positive or negative and needs the shortest continuous run of movements whose cumulative total reaches at least a required liquidity target, so they can raise the smallest possible block of funds quickly. Because movements can be negative, the simple positive-only window is invalid, and a correct general method is required. This is exactly the shortest-subarray-with-sum-at-least-k problem on signed data.

Problem 2 — Brute-force checking of every run is quadratic and cannot meet the desk's near-real-time needs. The prefix-sum-with-monotonic-deque method finds the shortest qualifying run in a single linear pass even with negatives, which is what lets the desk respond quickly.

The code has the shared `Account` class, an `IntradayLiquidityFinder` service with a `shortestRunToReach` method implementing the deque algorithm, and a runnable `ShortestSubarrayDemo` main class that runs Rajesh's and Priya's movement sequences against a target, logging deque operations at fine level and the shortest run at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's moves are 2, -1, 2 with target 3. First we build the prefix array of length four: prefix at 0 is 0, prefix at 1 is 2, prefix at 2 is 1, prefix at 3 is 3. We use an empty deque and a best of a large sentinel.

Step 1 at i equal 0, prefix 0: the deque is empty, no front pop and no back pop. We push index 0. Deque is now 0.

Step 2 at i equal 1, prefix 2: front check, prefix 2 minus prefix at front index 0 which is 0 equals 2, not at least 3, so no front pop. Back check, prefix at back index 0 is 0, which is not greater than or equal to 2, so no back pop. We push index 1. Deque is 0, 1.

Step 3 at i equal 2, prefix 1: front check, prefix 1 minus prefix at front 0 equals 1, not at least 3, no front pop. Back check, prefix at back index 1 is 2, which is greater than or equal to 1, so pop index 1. Now back is index 0 with prefix 0, not greater than or equal to 1, stop. We push index 2. Deque is 0, 2.

Step 4 at i equal 3, prefix 3: front check, prefix 3 minus prefix at front 0 which is 0 equals 3, at least 3, so record length 3 minus 0 equals 3, best becomes 3, pop front index 0. Now front is index 2 with prefix 1, prefix 3 minus 1 equals 2, not at least 3, stop. Back check, prefix at back index 2 is 1, not greater than or equal to 3, no back pop. We push index 3.

The shortest qualifying run for Rajesh is 3, the whole array summing to 3.

```
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Shortest run to reach 3 over [2, -1, 2] = 3
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Rajesh Kumar shortest run = 3
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Shortest run to reach 3 over [1, 1, 1] = 3
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Priya Sharma shortest run = 3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem asks for the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least k, in an array that may contain negatives, and because negatives break the simple positive-only sliding window I solve it with prefix sums and a monotonic deque in linear time. I build a prefix-sum array where any subarray sum is a difference of two prefixes, and for each right endpoint I want the latest left endpoint whose prefix is at most the current prefix minus k, which yields the shortest qualifying subarray ending there.

I process the prefixes left to right maintaining a deque of indices whose prefix values increase from front to back. Two pops keep it correct. From the front, while the current prefix minus the front prefix is at least k, I record the length and pop the front, because that left endpoint can never give a shorter subarray for any later right endpoint. From the back, while the back prefix is greater than or equal to the current prefix, I pop it, because a prefix that is higher and earlier is dominated by the current lower, later one as a left-endpoint candidate. Then I push the current index. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the whole pass is linear.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the intraday-liquidity desk. Net cash movements could be positive or negative, and we needed the shortest continuous run whose cumulative total reached at least a required liquidity target so we could raise the smallest possible block of funds quickly. The positive-only window was invalid because of the negatives, so the prefix-sum-with-monotonic-deque method gave the correct shortest run in a single linear pass, which was fast enough for the desk's near-real-time needs.

The senior-level point I make is that recognizing when the simple window fails, specifically the moment negatives can appear, and reaching for prefix sums plus a monotonic deque, is the real signal of depth here, because many candidates incorrectly apply the greedy window. I always justify both pops explicitly, the front because a satisfied left endpoint is never needed again and the back because a higher earlier prefix is strictly dominated, since being able to articulate that is what proves I understand why the algorithm is linear and correct. I also note that I use long prefixes to avoid overflow on monetary data. Explaining the failure of the naive window and the dual-pop invariant is exactly what distinguishes a candidate who has mastered this harder variant.
